Mr. F. L. S'CHAFFNER (Souris) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, an early opportunity should be taken to endeavour to have removed the embargo on Canadian cattle entering the British Isles.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to detain the House for more than a few moments in regard to this question of the removal of the embargo which has existed since 1892 on Canadian cattle entering the British market. Although this question has not been before the House of Commons recently, it is by no means a new oinie. ilmimiediattely 'after the embargo was placed upon Canadian cattle in 1892, members of the Federal House, some of whom are still members, brought forward long and very effective arguments why this embargo ishould never have existed, and why, after it was put into force, it should be removed. In 1905, the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. William Smith), who is still member for that Riding, Mr. T. S. Sproule, the then member for East Grey, and the hon. member for the St. Lawrence Division of Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike) who is laJiso stiil']) member for that oorustiiituieincy, made long and what should have been conclusive arguments why this embargo should cease to exist. I do not purpose repeating those arguments to-night, because I do not think that is necessary, but the time would: be well spent if the House were to discuss this question once more.
Previous to 1892, a very large cattle tr%de had grown up, especially in Ontario and western Canada, and in looking over the history of what has occurred since the embargo was put into force, I was surprised at the effect which that embargo had upon the Taising of stock in this country. Farmers and others who are engaged in this particular industry seem to have become discouraged, and it is remarkable how the number of cattle has diminished, and how discouraged the people have become in producing more stock. It may be argued that this is not an opportune time to discuss this question when prices are so high.
I micitice iini ito-diay's papier the statement itlhiait even tlhe packers of this country are suggesting that Qamiada should have two meatlesis daiyisiai week. I miajiintatn

and I have maikitadirued for ia yeair or two-that it is high time that the Canadian people and their representatives in this House began to think of the conditions which must occur

after the termination of the war. I believe that a short discussion on this question of the removal of the embargo and a request to the Government and the Minister of Agriculture, in particular, that special measures be taken for the removal of the embargo, will do much to enhance Canada's prosperity. There seems never to have been any good reason for the imposition of the embargo. The stated cause is that our cattle contain a disease called contagious pleuro-pneumonia, but I believe that one old cow out of all the cattle shipped to the old country was responsible and has been responsible for the condition in which we have been placed so far as our market for cattle in Great Britain is concerned. This subject is important as an after-the-war question, because I believe, so far as the raising of cattle is concerned, we are going to return to conditions somewhat similar to those which existed before 1892. A great many young men from western Canada and Ontario have gone out of banks and out of stores and have gone to the front, and I feel convinced that such young men, when they return, will not be content to go back to their indoor occupations, but will desire to go on the farms. Although that is not the opinion of every one, it is certainly mine. We have heard members of this Government and gentlemen who are not in the Government advocating a great increase in production. I am one of those who are very much pleased that we have free wheat, but I am also one of those who believe that in the future, when all our soldiers return and agriculture at once becomes, as it ought to be, the supreme occupation of Canada, the high prices that the farmer is receiving to-day will not be maintained. Just before the war the farmers in the West were not getting, by any means, paying prices for wheat, because 70 or 80 or 90 cents a bushel will not, under any condition, prove a paying proposition. We hear some members of the Government, and some gentlemen who are outside of the Government and outside of this House continually advocating mixed farming. No one can gainsay the advantages of mixed farming, because tlhe argument is absolutely sound that we should not put all our efforts into the raising of wheat-and I am speaking now more particularly of western Canada, although perhaps the same argument applies to Ontario and the eastern provinces. After the war wheat will not remain at the present high price, and perhaps it will not command even a paying price.

Thus it may become necessary for us to go in for mixed farming, *which, to speak plainly, consists of growing wheat and raising different kinds of stock, and it is u.p to us right now to 'have this embargo removed .if possible.
Before taking my isea't, I should like to quote .something ithiait was placed! oin Hansard many years ago, in 1893, in reference to this poor old cow that was accused of having had pleuro-pneumonia, and which has been responsible for the embargo ever since; and while on this point, let me say it was proved by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) and by others who spoke at that time, that Canada possessed the cleanest record in regard to the health of our cattle of any country in the world, and the same is true to-day. I took the pains of consulting Dr. Torrance, the Veterinary Director General of Canada, and he told me that we have not, and never have had, any pleuro-pneumonia among our cattle.
What was the cause of all this trouble? It seems that the cattle that iwe call Stockers were formerly taken over to Great Britain, where, on the splendid English pastures, they developed into the very finest of beef. Our cattle when finished were superior to any that came from Ireland, that great agricultural country which has produced so many cattle; and I am convinced, after reading all the arguments, and according to the best information that I ©an get, that the embargo was purely a case of self-interest and self-protection om the part of the Irish rather than because of any danger of pleuropneumonia. In the Sessional Papers of 1893 we learn that:
A portion of the lungs of the affected animal was sent to Principal Williams and Professor W. G. Williams of the new veterinary college, Edinburgh, and naked-eye microscopic examination convinced those experts that bronchopneumonia, (the well-known cornstalk disease of America,) had been mistaken for pleuropneumonia contagiosa. I have subsequently examined the lungs and microscopic sections made from them, and I had no difficulty in recognizing that the pathological appearances presented were identical with those of the cornstalk disease, which I had the opportunity of seeing in Washington in 1890 by the courtesy of Dr. D. E. Salmon, the distinguished chief of the bureau of animal industry of the United States. The differences in the post-mortem appearances and in the actual seats of the two diseases, make it extremely unlikely for any one versed in morbid anatomy to mistake the one for the other. In pleuro-pneumonia contagiosa the true seat of the disease is not in the bronchial tubes, although the smaller of these become gorged with an inflammatory coagulated exudate.
Broncho-pneumonia, not unknown in this country, is not a specific disease like pleuropneumonia contagiosa, but one which originates spontaneously when animals are exposed to cold and wet, especially after being heated, as cattle are during transit by rail and sea. It may fitly be compared with influenza in the human species, not of the recent epidemic type, but of the old and familiar form of a severe cold.
That was the opinion of one of the most eminent scientific men in England at that time. The embargo, however, was put on, and it was impossible for us to send our cattle over to England to be finished as we had done formerly. Our farmers used to have a very profitable market in the Old Country not only for finished beef, hut also for short-keeps, which were sent over to England and finished on the splendid pasturage there.
What happened when this embargo was put on by England? A large number of breeders in Ontario and the West were at that time asaiiisliing ehont-keap ©aititle far export, and they were compelled to hold them here as they were not finished sufficiently for export. Trainloads of calves were shipped to Winnipeg, killed and placed in cold storage. The same thing occurred in Calgary and Toronto. Great numbers of our young cattle have been shipped across the line to the United States in recent years. Our American friends realize how excellent and profitable Canadian-raised cattle are, and American buyers are to be found on the Toronto and Winnipeg stock yards buying all the young cattle they can get. J have some figures here of the Toronto and Winnipeg stock yards and find that from Winnipeg 1,306 head were shipped in the month of June, 1916; in July, 1,564; in August, 4,895; in September, 6,977; in October, 9,087; a total from Winnipeg to the United States of 23,829 in five months.
It might be asked why I am bringing up this question now, with prices so high and cattle so scarce. My object is entirely for the benefit of the farmers of this country and of our	young	men. As	you
know, Sir, Canada is to-day sending thousands of her best young men overseas to fight in the cause of freedom. They are over in France to-day fighting the baltitile of iliibemty By-tansd-by itbey Villi come back. I feel that I should 'be remiss in my duty if I did not raise my voice, i'f I did not do the best I can in my humble way, to make provision for the occupation for these young men when they return. I say this resolution is opportune, for, it seems to me, never in the history of the Empire did Great Britain recognize as she does to-day what Canada is and what the

name Canada means. I believe that Great Britain can be approached to-day in the interest of this great Dominion as never before, and. perhaps, no such opportunity will ever offer again. I am sure that it is the opinion of every member of this House that this Government, through the Minister of Agriculture, should put forth every effort to the end that this embargo upon our Canadian cattle, which has existed since 1892, and, as I claim, has existed unjustly, should be removed, and that we may once more have the freedom of the markets of Great Britain.

speechtext:
Though this question is an old one, as the hon. member for Souris has said, it is a question that is very much alive. The facts are substantially as my hon. friend has related them, and as they have been touched upon by the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike). There was an alleged case of pleuro-pneu-monia in 1892, but I do not think that there has been any doubt in men's minds since then that it was only an alleged case, and that the examination which took place proved absolutely that there was no case of contagious pleuro-pneumonia. Within the next few years after the imposition of the embargo, no fewer than 3,000,000 head of Canadian cattle were sent to the British market and slaughtered on arrival, and not one of them showed evidences of disease. Since then, as has been pointed out, not only has the .case been debated in this House, but representations have been made by the Canadian Government on various occasions, and also, as my hon. friend has pointed out, by delegations from Scotland and various parts of England, in favour of the removal of the embargo as being against the interests even of the Scotch and English agriculturists. However, the several British Governments have seen fit to retain the embargo, which I might say was made statutory within two or three years after it was first placed, and has been kept in that position ever since. It did not seem worth while to argue very much, for the authorities there took the ground the embargo was justified by the danger to their own herds of the disease being brought from this country. It was spoken of as purely a matter of health. I am not going to touch on the point raised by my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Lawrence, because I do not think it is my bfisiness to say what motives may or may not be imputed to our kinsmen on the other side of the water. But I can say that the ground they took, that the embargo was justified as a health measure, was Pot sound. The right hon. leader of th'e Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) when Prime Minister, took up this matter at one of the Imperial Conferences, and brought it before the Minister of Agriculture, that office being held at that time, I think, by Mr. Long. The British authorities took the position that, with a border line three thousand miles long for Canada to guard, and there being many cattle diseases in the United
States, it was especially necessary that they should take any necessary means to safeguard the health of their animals against any possible importation of disease from the United States via Canada.
I might point out to the House that while we have never had a disease of the first class and contagious character, such as pleuro-pneumonia, or foot and mouth disease, in Canada, our friends on the other side of the water, who embargo us, have a great many times had serious diseases for which we have been compelled to embargo them. In reference to the condition of our cattle and the danger of disease 'from the United States, I would like to point out to the House, because it is interesting, that they have had no less than three outbreaks of foot and mouth disease in the United States, the last of which was of an extraordinarily serious character, lasting nearly a year, and entailing the slaughter of thousands of cattle and inflicting a loss of millions of dollars on the various states and the federal authorities of the United States. In spite of that, owing to the vigilance of our own veterinary service, and the extraordinary precautions which we thought we were justified in taking, we came out at the end of the outbreak with absolutely not a single case in the whole of Canada. That is why I say that the argument that they have tried to sustain has proved absolutely unsound. There has been nothing gained practically by pressing this matter very much of late years from the fact that it was taken up on a number of occasions, but the attitude of the British Government was such that it became scarcely a dignified matter to press it further, because it Was a matter entirely within their own jurisdiction. The last time that it was taken up was, I think, in 1913, when I had an informal talk with the Right Honourable Walter Runci-man, who was president of the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries. We discussed the question pretty thoroughly, but it was quite obvious that there was no good in pressing the matter officially any further, and so we let it drop.
There will be no two opinions as to the desirability of removing this embargo in so far as the embargo reflects upon the health of the herds of this country. It does reflect upon them to a certain extent. While there cannot be any two opinions on that point, because there is no justification for the embargo on that ground, I am quite aware that there may possibly be a difference of opinion as to the economic results

which followed the imposition of the embargo and the economic results which may follow its removal. It is true, as the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) pointed out, that there are some people in this country who think that the embargo was perhaps not an unmixed evil in that it led to the finishing of our cattle and therefore helped the fertility of the farm. I am sure also that it helped to build up our great packing industry, and led undoubtedly to the strengthening of the big export trade in meats which also is a very important question. Nevertheless, I would like to put myself on record in this House as believing that the stability of our cattle industry, which, I think is of supreme importance tp the agriculture of this country, would be benefited by the removal of the embargo because it is desirable that the farmer should have two outlets, that he should be able to sell his product for export as well as to the packing houses. As a matter of fact, the western farmer and the eastern farmer have sold a good many stackers to the United States which trade we have tried to counteract this year as far as we could and I am glad to say that there has been a notable change in that regard and that a very large number of cattle at the Winnipeg and other markets which otherwise would have been disposed for slaughter, or have gone to the United States, have been bought in and sent back to the Canadian western farms.
I believe it would be a permanent benefit to have the embargo removed. The depletion of the herds of Europe that is going on now is appalling and must have its effect in every part of the wprld. In France, especially, and, of course, in Belgium, Serbia, and other countries which have 'been ravished by our common enemy, that de-plettikm has to .be made up aindf it. will take a long time to make it up. I doubt not that in so far as this continent may be able to supply it, there will be a strong demand for cattle of all kinds, especially in France and Belgium, after this war is over, and we hope it will be finished by driving the common foe out of those countries. As France has not been disposed to impose any restriictiioinj, they apparently, hawing no fault to find with our cattle, it would be regrettable if the Government of Great Britain should maintain a restriction against one of her dominions against which France and her other Allies impose no restriction whatever.
May I say to the House, and to my hon. friend who brought up this resolution, that

when my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (.Sir Robert Borden) left for England to take up, first, questions affecting the war, second, questions regarding the making of peace and, third, problems 'after the war, he asked the various members of the Government to put before him any statement of questions that they thought it important we should have taken up. It seemed 'to me that from the point of view of agriculture, there was no more important question than the one which my hon. friend has brought up, and so I took the opportunity to prepare a very careful case, or brief, on the whole subject dealing with it from its origin in 1892. I think we left no argument untouched and put the matter in .such shape that the Prime Minister would be able 'to lay it before the British Government in the hope that we would be [DOT]able to make some headway at this particular time.
I do not altogether agree with my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike). because, although I know that the efforts that he and many others have made, have not met with very much response, I am not altogether as sceptical as he is at this particular time. I believe that this is the psychological moment and for various reasons which I am not now going to touch on, I think there is strong hope that the British Government, at this particular time, may see their way to do what they have not been inclined to do for twenty-four years, and that the result may be the removal of the embargo. I am quite hopeful of it. I want to assure my hon. friend again that the matter has been placed before the Prime Minister in the strongest possible way, and | am confident that he will put it before the Imperial authorities in an equally strong way. I will not say more than that, because, after all, it is within their right and within their power to do as they like; it is a domestic matter, and whatever may he our views we have to abide by their decision. In view of what I have said. I will ask my hon. friend, as this practically fulfils the spirit of his resolution, if he would be good enough to withdraw it, because we have already taken the question up and dealt with it in a way that we hope will give practical results.

I see no reason, why this resolution should not be adopted as expressing the opinion of this House. I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike) that whether we adopt it or not it will have very little effect

upon the results. I would be very sorry, indeed, as a Canadian citizen and a member of the House, if there was any disposition on the part of the people of this country, after this w.ar, to go to Great Britain and use as an argument to get something we want our participation in this great struggle. I do not think that position will be taken. My hon. friend from St. Lawrence is a little bit wrong in his diagnosis of the cause of the trouble. That may ibe attributed to the fact that he has had [DOT] little experience along medical lines, and. therefore, is not practised in the art of diagnosis. He said that the trouble was not due to the disease of pleuro-pneumonia, but to a disease called protection. I think he would have been more nearly correct had he said that the disease was free trade as they have it in England. I might remind my hon. friend, if he will accept- my correction of [DOT]has diagnosis ialk).ng ibhiait (Mme, ithiait iait one time that was a battle -cry of the party he supported. What was really the reason w'hy Great Britain placed this embargo upon our cattle? I think the hon. Minister of Agriculture suggested the reason without putting it in plain words, being a very modest man. Let us look back to the time when the embargo was placed upon our cattle in 1892. In 1891 there was a political party in this country declaring for unrestricted reciprocity, for breaking down all tariff walls between Canada and the United States. British statesmen, whatever may be said of them, cannot be characterized as men who are not alive to what is going on in the world around them. They no douibt looked the situation over as it was in Canada, and while they were not apprehensive of any danger to their herds from any disease in Canada, they naturally thought that if an irresponsible party like the Grit party was to get into power, take down the tariff walls and allow American cattle to come in here free, as that disease was rampant .among American cattle they would, by admitting cattle from Canada free, be opening their doors to cattle from both Canada and the United States. At this time when English statesmen were wondering how to get out of this great difficulty some person-I do not attribute this to the hon. member for St. Lawrence (Mr. Bickerdike), who is in the export trade-sent over an old cow showing some symptoms of disease, and the British Government said: Now, this is our opportunity,1 we are a free trade country and all that, we have to have an excuse to offer, and while the danger that we are apprehensive of is that this Liberal
party will get into power and remove the barriers, allowing American diseased cattle to come free into Canada, we must protect ourselves against the possibility of this party coming into power in Canada; this old cow which had been sent over by some exporters from Montreal or elsewhere has provided us with the excuse we want; we will simply raise that as the cry, that we are afraid of disease in Canadian cattle, and we will put an embargo on. I think possibly that is the true estimation of why this was done. It was really a measure of protection on the part of a free trade Government such as they have in England. It was a part of a policy known to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House as free trade as they have it in England which, -of course, was inscribed on their banner for one election. They will bear me out when I say that they have had a new motto inscribed on their banner for every election.

The day may come when mixed farming will play a part and will possibly be the great hope of our western farmers, and they will go in extensively for the breeding of cattle. It appears to me that to-day we would not hear so much about free wheat if the Canadian western farmer had been alive to his larger interests. speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that no further appointments be made to the Senate of Canada until after the next Federal elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I move this resolution not as an academic question, but rather as a practical question, to be fairly considered by this House, and I would ask

for a fair expression of the opinion and judgment of the House upon it. The resolution is a fair, just and timely one and should be accepted by the House; and from the Government we should have a declaration of acceptance of the principles which it sets forth.
On October 7, 1916, the present Parliament would have ended had it not been for the fact that during the last session of Parliament an Act was passed in the form of an amendment to the British North America Act extending the term of this Parliament for the period of one year. Since October 7, 1917, this Parliament has been a war emergency Parliament and the Government a war emergency Government. It was the obvious intention of Parliament and, I think, the opinion of hon. gentlemen of this House who voted upon the resolution favouring the extension of Parliament, that the business which should engage Parliament and the Government during the year's extension should relate entirely to war, the incidents of war, and such civil affairs as, in the interest of the State, required immediate action by Parliament or the Government. It would appear, upon reference to the speech delivered to Parliament upon the opening of the session by His Excellency, that the purpose of the extension was to enable the Government to carry on during that period the affairs relating to the war without encountering the distractions of an election. Upon that ground the question was placed before hon. gentlemen and ft was with such circumstances in view that the House consented unanimously to the extension of the twelfth Parliament of Canada for one year beyond the constitutional period. The wisdom of this extension was doubted by some. It was thought by many hon. gentlemen, although that opinion was not expressed in Parliament, that the extension might do violence to the well-settled provisions of the British North America Act, which is our constitution. That was the view held by some hon. gentlemen opposite. During the debate on the extension of Parliament resolution last session, some hon. gentlemen referred to a statement made by the Minister of Public Works, some time previous to the occasion to which I refer. It was his view that the people of Canada were being robbed of tbeir rights and liberties because the Government were not appealing to the people. The statement, of the Mfnister of Public Works, then read to Parliament, was as follows:

Is it, then, any wonder that the cry comes, from every individual that one meets and that understands the conditions, in tones louder than thunder, demanding that this Parliament be dissolved, that the rights and liberties of the people of this Dominion be granted to them under our form of democracy and that that form of democracy be restored to them?
The Minister of Public Works evidently felt very strongly against an extension of Parliament. He thought that to abstain from an appeal to the people was an unjustifiable attack upon democracy. Possibly his views at that time were rather extreme, and were not shared by many hon. gentlemen in this House. In any event, the extension of Parliament was unanimously granted, solely for the purpose, as I have said, of enabling the Government to carry on the affairs of state specifically referable to the war, free from the distractions and turmoil of an election. It was hoped that after the expiration of the extension the situation in Europe would be such as to permit the Government to make an appeal to the people.
Many vacancies have occurred in the House of Commons since the extension of Parliament was granted. During a period arranged between the parliamentary leaders, vacancies caused by death or otherwise were filled by the election of a member holding the same political views as the former representative of the constituency. It is my recollection
9 p.m. that this arrangement, which was a fair one, was not fully carried out. Some differences, I think, occurred between the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government and the right hon. leader of the Opposition as to the proper course to be pursued in the event of a voluntary or enforced vacancy. I think they were unable to come to a clear understanding as to the exact meaning of the arrangement they had made in its application to such cases. During the last year and a half or two years no vacancy occurring in the House of Commons has been filled unless it was a vacancy occurring by the elevation of a member to the Cabinet. There are many vacancies to-day in the Commons, but I doubt if anybody feels deeply aggrieved because of that. The rule, just or unjust, applies to both political parties; therefore very little has been said about it.
Hon. gentlemen know that our Parliament is composed of two bodies, a Senate and the House of Commons, the members of the latter being elected by the people and those of the former being appointed by the Crown on the recommendation of the Executive.
My resolution asks for a declaration that from now on until the election of a new Parliament no further appointments be made by the Government to the Senate. It is so eminently reasonable that it mu3t impress hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House that no other arrangement is fair to the country or to an Opposition. If no vacancies in the House of Commons are filled by reason of an arrangement between the party leaders, that rule should apply with equal force to vacancies occurring in the Senate, namely, that there should be no appointments made, or, if any are made, that the vacancies should be filled by the nominees of the party leaders, in accordance with the same rule as was in force in this branch of Parliament for a time at least.
An Opposition is a constitutional institution; it is a part of the establishment of the Government; it is a part of the fundamental law of this country and of all other portions of the British Empire. The Opposition is referred to frequently by speakers in and out of Parliament as His Majesty's Loyal Opposition, and its rights have been well established and recognized for a great number of years in the constitutional history of the British Empire. It is unfair that during that period, that is, from the 7th day of October, 1916, up to the dissolution of Parliament, that the party -which is in office Iby f!he grace of am Opposition parity 'Should exercise .the niighit which ilt wiouilid ordlilniardily properly exiercise, of making lappoiinitimieintsi to- the ISemaibe of Cainiadiai. I oanmet comiceive of iany argument that can be adviainiceid .agiaiimBt my eomibenltiiiomi ;if^ is simply 'applying to the (Senate the terms of the agreement made between the party leaders in respect of vacancies in this branch of Parliament. It is not fair for the dominant political party, in office by the grace of the Opposition party, under an extension of the Parliamentary term, granted to them for one purpose alone, to take upon themselves the making of appointments to the Senate. I trust that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House will look at the matter in the same way as I do, and if so, there will be little doubt as to the course this House should pursue this evening in respect to this resolution. I do not think it is necessary that I should say anything further upon itba rcBofaitioini. Bt is so eminently fair that I trust some member of the Government, speaking for hon. gentlemen on the other side, will immediately say that

the principle of the resolution is accepted. I cannot ask the Government to revoke appointments that they have recently made to the Senate, although I submit, in all fairness, that those appointments were unfairly made in pursuance of a power which should have been left in abeyance, if justice were to be done to the Opposition party.
My attention has been called to a fact which I had forgotten, namely, that in request to the western provinces, the power has been bestowed upon the Government of making additional appointments to the Senate just prior to dissolution, and I understand that that power was confirmed by an Act of the British Parliament. I am not clear in my mind as to the exact course which Parliament took in respect of this matter; but at least, I assume that hon. gentlemen opposite understand the mattter to which. I lefer. If by Statute or otherwise the Government had the power granted to them prior to the war and prior to the extension of Parliament, one could not fairly ask that the Government forego the right of making those appointments. That is a power granted to them by Statute prior to the extension of Parliament, and it is one which I hardly think hon. gentlemen on this side of the House could very well ask the Government now to forego. Therefore, I feel that I should amend my resolution by adding to it the following words, which I think express what I have in mind:
Excepting, however, the additional appointments to be made from the western provinces of Canada prior to the dissolution of Parliament.
I beg to move the resolution as amended.
My attention has just been called to the fact that the Act which provides for the appointment of additional senators to the Senate of Canada to represent the group of western provinces does not take effect until the termination of the now existing Canadian Parliament, and, of course, if that is correct, there is no necessity of my amending the resolution, and consequently I shall not have to amend it.

The appointments to the Senate of Canada are made on the recommendation of the Governor in Council, and under the constitution of Canada are part of the duty of the Government. speechtext:
And in the Commons
as well. As the hon. member has his mind on the Commons, I might as well touch on that phase of the subject first. There are at the present time, I believe, about fifteen or sixteen vacancies in the House of Commons. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Miacfeam) Aa I believe ooirireat that for some time after the outbreak of war vacancies were filled by acclamation, the acclamations taking place in accordance with, an understanding that the candidate so elected should toe of the party that the retiring or deceased candidate belonged to. That practice was followed for some time. The hon. member states that then there was some misunderstanding as to the continuance of the practice. Well, I do not know that "misunderstanding" is the word that properly describes it. The subject fortunately is dealt with in correspondence that passed between the leader of the Government and the leader of the Opposition. The leader of the Government proposed that the election of members to this House should continue unconditionally along that line. It was his desire in furtherance of his well-known attitude to prevent schism and federal electoral contests during the war, that by-elections should be avoided. As a consequence he made the proposal, in writing, that vacancies should be filled according to that

method. The leader of the Opposition, in the exercise of his right, did not see fit to accede. As part of another arrangement, however, he did agree that the practice should be followed in part, and part only, namely, in the case of vacanies caused by death, tout not in the case of vacancies caused by resignation. That was his election; that was his choice. That being the case, vacancies caused by resignation, if they were to be filled at all, would have to be filled only after election contests, which it was the desire of the Government, and which I think it is the desire of the people of Canada, should be avoided. As to the responsibility for that choice, the leader of the Opposition took it; it was his right; but the responsibility is hiss and his alone. As a consequence, there are a number of vacancies in this House. There are a number in the West, a number in the central provinces, and a number in the East, but the West is under-represented in the Commons on that account. Furthermore, Western Canada is under-represented in the Commons by reason of a growth in the population of that country, and the fact that the British North America Act provides for a revision only upon a decennial census. The continuance of this Parliament intensifies that situation, and as a matter of fact there is to-day a very, very substantial under-representation of the four western provinces as a result. I agree with the hon. member for Halifax that in the western' country, as in other provinces, we are prepared to forego our rights in that regard with the idea that we achieve a greater object in the avoidance of an election in time of war. However, the fact remains, and it has its import with respect to the resolution.
As to the Senate, the West is again very much under represented, and I do not hesitate to say that the responsibility in this regard lies with hon. gentlemen opposite, or rather I should say with hon. gentlemen above. Some four years ago an address was introduced in this House looking to the amendment of the British North America Act, with the object of securing for the four westerm provinces a normal (approach to a more equitable representation in the Upper House than they had heretofore enjoyed. This, of course, was necessitated by the increase in population, which had been so marked in that section of Canada. Up to then Manitoba was represented in the Senate by four, Saskatchewan by four, Alberta by four, and British Columbia by three; and as against that Ontario had
twenty-four representatives in the Senate, and Quebec twenty-four. The Maritime Provinces had their numbers fixed by Confederation, twenty-four for the three provinces, the three together being on a parity with either of the two major provinces. The address at that time was to provide that there should be six representatives from Manitoba, six from Alberta, six from Saskatchewan, and six, I believe, from British Columbia; that is to say, there was an increase of fifty per cent, or of two members for each of the four western provinces. The Bill was introduced in 1912; I may be wrong, it might have been early in 1913, but my recollection would place it in the year 1912-a long time, it will be observed, before the war broke out. The Bill passed this House with the consent of both parties, I believe, and went to the Senate, where, at the dictation of the Senate majority, it was mutilated to this extent: they felt, for some reason that never found any lodgment in my mind as a logical one, or I might use a stronger term, Mr. Speaker, if I were not in the House, that it should not go into effect until the termination of the present Parliament of Canada. Why it would be right on the termination of this Parliament, and wrong at that time, the under-representation being most emphatic when the Bill was before the Senate, is very hard indeed to conceive. The responsibility for that constitutionally is upon the Senate itself, but as a matter of fact the responsibility is on that portion of the Senate of Canada whose political sympathies are in accord with those of hon. gentlemen opposite. On them rests the responsibility of depriving four provinces of this Confederation for four long years of their fair representation in the Upper Chamber. The province of British Columbia, for example, has at the present time one representative in the Senate, and if this resolution were passed that province would have to be content to remain with this solitary representative, while the province of Prince Edward Island, whose population is very small compared to that of British Columbia, and the other provinces east of Manitoba have the representation they have. Surely that could not be argued as just to British Columbia; a more gross and palpable injustice could scarcely be inflicted.

Now, the hon. member argues that the extension of Parliament was eriven as a matter of grace. I do not think I should comment on that further than to say that when the resolution for extension was introduced, it was stated by the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) in laneuase the purpose of which, if not the words, I remember, ithiait ilt was tmoit being asked as a matter of grace or because of our needs, but was simply .submitted to this House, and particularly to the members of the Opposition, and they were to decide whether they deemed it in the interests of this country that that extension should be granted, having regard to the times we were passing through. I apprehend that it being granted, the rights, duties, and obligations of the Government remain exactly as they were before. One of the duties of the Government is to see to it that the Upper Chamber is, within such reasonable limits as may be allowed, kept at its strength. The hon. gentleman says the extension was given only to enable the Government to conduct such of its business as appertains to the war. I cannot accede to that. The Government was absolved from no duty whatsoever by the extension of the term of Parliament. True, its duties with regard to war were primary and paramount, but it could not be said to be released frpm its other duties each in its pro-[Mr. Meighen.p
per order and subordination. Let me cite a plain illustration. One of the duties of the Government is to see to it that the judiciary is properly maintained, numerically and in point of qualification. Can it be said that if vacancies exist on the bench they should not be filled, because the extension of the term of Parliament was given to enable the Government to continue the war? I might give many other illustrations of the same character and which the hon. gentleman must admit are exactly in line with appointments to the Senate, unless he is prepared to say .that filling vacancies in the Senate is purely a matter of party patronage. I would suggest that to place the Senate on that footing is not to maintain that respect for the Upper House which the rules of this House call for.

The passing of the resolution would leave a large portion of the country in a condition of gross under-representation, in the Senate even more gross than that which it suffers under by reason of the actipn of friends of hon. gentlemen opposite in this House. Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew) : This question, as the Solicitor Generali (Mr. Meighem) hiae .aaiiid, .its .a very important one. main, whichever party is in power, that party notices that the 'best men to go into the Senate are its own supporters. Call that by any name you like, but I would not for a moment say that it was derogatory to the Senate, because I am of the opinion that, on the whole, the Upper Chamber of Canada is a great credit to the country, and that its members bring to the consideration of many questions that we discuss in this House a mature experience and utnlbiiaised judgment ,wlhiiich, perhaps, 'sometimes some of us in the heat of political conflict might not possess. The Solicitor General has referred to the question of the under-representation of the West in the Senate, but I would call his attention to the fact that the West is under-represented also in the House of Commons. My hon. friend argues that a portion of this Parliament ought to have new representation from the West, but the other portion is debarred under the British North America Act from having any similar increase. In other words, that the branch of Parliament which is appointed by the Government should be filled up to its capacity while the people should be deprived of having their representation sent to the House of Commons. The Government, in the words of my hon. friend, has the right to do that thing, but they say that the people ought to be deprived of their representation in the other Chamber. The reason for which the Senate made a certain amendment, I think, is quite clear. As stated by the Solicitor General, this extra representation comes after the decennial census is taken. That is why there is a shortage of representation in the West in both Houses. The Senate takes the ground, and rightly so, that this new 59

They did add an amendment which is not unfair to the people, but which is eminently fair to the people, and much fairer to the people than that the Government should send its appointees to the Senate while the people were deprived of the right to send their representatives to the House of Commons. What does the section say:
The first section of this Act, paragraphs 1 to 6 inclusive, shall not take effect until the termination of the now existing Canadian Parliament.
I am not going to argue when that time arrives, but one thing is sure, that this Government accepted that amendment when it said that new appointments to the Senate fricim western Oaraaidia could miaft 'be made till after the dissolution of Parliament. Some eminent lawyers say that these appointments could not be made until the new Parliament is elected. I leave that to the House to discuss. But, it is certain that new appointments cannot be made until after the dissolution takes place. I think that is not unfair.
The Solicitor General gave an outline of a certain arrangement or understanding that had taken place between the two leaders. In the main I think he was correct although he adroitly attributed-I would not say motives-but a certain frame of mind to the leader of the Opposition, although he admitted that he had a right to be in that frame of mind if he so desired. manner in which they had become vacant.

tlemen without a contest. These are the constituencies that were in question. The Minister of Labour has exceedingly heavy duties devolving upon him in connection with this war. How it would be possible to carry on a general election with the duties, urgent, immediate, and all-important, devolving upon ministers of the Crown at the time an extension was granted, I think no one can conceive. Those were the grounds,

and in addition to those grounds the further ground of the public turmoil and the excitement that would take place over this country and the diversion of the activities of the people from the war, the all-important question of the hour, to the hustings and an election campaign, with the ensuing disturbance, not to say the ill-will that might result. All those considerations apply to contested elections to the House of Commons because it is the people's Chamber, but not at all to appointments to the Senate. The Government of the day is empowered, authorized and obligated under the constitution to fill vacancies in the Senate, and that is what this Government has been doing. It is one of the ordinary duties devolving upon Government, and the Government is discharging it, and would not, I think, be justified in undertaking to refrain from discharging it. The mere fact that some party advantage may accrue to this side or some disadvantage to the other side is at this time of no national significance. Mr. Speaker, from the outbreak of hostilities to the present moment, I think it has been

possible to contend that every Canadian whose patriotism was at once strong and enlightened, had one object before him, altogether paramount to anything else that could occupy us as public men in this country, and that object is the winning of the war. Another proposition can be laid down as to the method by which that object could best be obtained. For the winning of the war, it was absolutely necessary for strong and enlightened men to combine, irrespective of previous differences, to preserve the national unity. Those propositions are obvious. They prevail in Germany; they prevail in Britain; they are not questioned there for a moment. When the question of the extension of the term of Parliament came before us last year, these considerations animated both sides of the House. I would not say that the Government are in power by the grace of the Opposition; I do not think that is quite a fair way to put it; the government are in power under an extended term of Parliament because last year the Opposition shared with the Government the two views which I have just said are the views which have prevailed with Canadians whose patriotism was at once strong and enlightened once the war broke out. It was perfectly obvious that for a continuance of those conditions'-and I agree with my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that the general question of extension will , be far better discussed when it is again before Parliament-it is necessary that there should be give and take between the two sides of this House, because after all whence does the threat to national unity come? It must come and can come only from an outbreak of partisanship. That is possible on the part of an Opposition; it is obviously equally possible on the part of the Government benches, and the duty to refrain from partisanship on the part of the Opposition must be enforced upon the Opposition by the example and the conduct of the Government and their supporters. I think that my reasoning up to this point would require my hon. friend the Solicitor General in his very best form to puncture it, even by methods of which I am not at all sure that he always approves himself. It is no use speaking to plain men about appointments to the Senate being the same as appointments to the judiciary. Of course, during the war, it goes without saying that the judiciary must go on, and I should be sorry to think that appointments to the judiciary are largely political

at any rate in any British country; but as my bom. friend' from Souith Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has pointed out, there is such a uniform course of action in regard to appointments to the Senate that a strong suspicion of partisanship regarding the matter does arise. The two cases are not alike. There is really strong ground for suspicion that appointments to the Senate are very generally political. I do not put this thing on the ground of the interest of the Government. I do not say the Government are in power by the grace of the Opposition; they are in power during an extended term of Parliament on a mutual understanding that party politics should be dropped and that the Government and the Opposition should achieve glory for their position in history as politicians and as statesmen by dropping their politics and uniting for a common purpose of paramount importance. All things are lawful to me, but all things are not expedient.	Is it wise for
the Government	who, I take it,
assent to every proposition I have laid down hitherto, to offer provocations to the Opposition that are only human? Is it in accordance with the general principles animating the country, animating the people, and, I hold, animating Parliament last year? I put it on that ground. Is it a wise thing? Ig it not certain to have the effect of leading the political parties to lock horns and destroy the national unity, and to that extent interfere, I would say terribly if not monstrously, with Canada's efficiency in the prosecution of the war? I do not want, in the words I am using, to refer to conditions in the spring of 1915 at all. I am too intent, Sir, upon the main objects which I say command the attention of Canadians at this time to want to refer to that. I am glad to be able to say that the Government, for some reason or another, did not have an election anyhow, and I am prepared to give them credit for that. The country knows perfectly well, of course, that there were members of the Government at that time who were thinking in terms of elections. I do not think it possible to convey any other impression to the country than that. I do not want to be unfair to anyone, but' that speech on the Senate could not \eave any doubt in any reasonable mind as to what the emergency man of the Administration was thinking about anyhow. But I noticed from their countenances that many of the other members of the Administration from the Prime Minister downwards were filled with doubts
as to the procedure of the emergency man. That I took to be the psychology of the Cabinet at the moment. I do not think cabinets always agree, not for a moment, but the fact remains and will go down in history that the Government did not have an election, and from that day on they have kept reasonably before them-and I have conceded it fully to them from this side of the House-the objects which I have said ought to command the consensus and agreement of Canadian opinion at this time. Now, in view of that, I would ask the Government to hold over a final decision on this question, if need be, until the Prime Mimisiteir returns, .and umltiil the subject can be carefully discussed and considered in the Cabinet. Because, after all, if an election comes, tremendous blame will be attached by the country to the party which brings on that election if it comes at a time when our men aTe falling in thousands, and when it is bound to have the effect of harming to- a dreadful extent the national unity.
I think the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) made an admirable speech in presenting this resolution, a speech of very great moderation, and of very strong reason. I do not think that what he advanced has been met by the speeches we have beard from, the other side and I would ask the Government to give the most careful consideration to the views I have tried to put before them in these few words.
